# Flow as controlled movement through a network

A flow network has capacities on directed edges. Dinic's algorithm repeats:
build a BFS level graph, then send blocking flow by DFS along increasing
levels. Bipartite matching is a special case of flow, and a minimum cut is
the set of vertices still reachable from the source in the residual graph
after max flow.

## Flow definitions

Each directed edge `(u, v)` has capacity `c(u, v)`. A feasible flow assigns a
number `f(u, v)` to each edge such that:

- `0 <= f(u, v) <= c(u, v)`;
- every vertex except source `s` and sink `t` has equal incoming and outgoing
  flow.

The value of the flow is the total amount leaving `s`.

Residual capacity tells us how we can still change the flow:

```text
forward residual: c(u,v) - f(u,v)
backward residual: f(u,v)
```

The backward edge is essential. It represents undoing or rerouting previous
flow.

## Dinic's algorithm

Dinic works in phases.

1. BFS from `s` using only positive residual edges. This gives `level[v]`.
2. DFS sends flow only along edges where `level[to] == level[v] + 1`.
3. The DFS continues until no more flow can be sent in this level graph.
4. Repeat BFS.

The level graph prevents DFS from wandering in cycles and gives a clear
progress measure. The pointer array `it[v]` remembers which outgoing edges
have already been exhausted during the current BFS phase.

Diagram:

```text
s --level 0
|\
v v
level 1 nodes
|    \
v     v
level 2 nodes ... t
```

DFS only moves left-to-right through increasing levels.

## Bipartite matching as flow

For a bipartite graph with left side `L` and right side `R`:

```text
source -> every left vertex      capacity 1
left u -> right v if edge exists capacity 1
every right vertex -> sink       capacity 1
```

Every unit of flow corresponds to one matched pair. Capacity `1` ensures each
vertex is used at most once.

For the local matching exercise we use the classic augmenting-path DFS because
it is shorter and exposes the same idea: try to give a left vertex a right
partner, recursively moving an already matched left vertex if possible.

## Minimum cut after max flow

After max flow, run BFS/DFS from `s` in the residual graph. Let `S` be the set
of reachable vertices. There is no residual edge from `S` to outside `S`;
otherwise the outside vertex would be reachable. The saturated original edges
crossing from `S` to `V-S` form a minimum cut, and its capacity equals the max
flow value.

This is the max-flow min-cut theorem in the form most useful in contests.

## Implementation checklist

- Store reverse-edge indices, not just reverse endpoints.
- When sending `x` through an edge, subtract `x` from the forward residual and
  add `x` to the reverse residual.
- Use `long long` for capacities and total flow in C++.
- Rebuild `level` every phase.
- Reset `it` after each BFS.

## Tiny max-flow trace

Network:

```text
s -> a capacity 3
s -> b capacity 2
a -> t capacity 2
b -> t capacity 4
a -> b capacity 1
```

One maximum flow has value `4`:

```text
s->a->t sends 2
s->b->t sends 2
```

The remaining capacity from `a` to `b` does not help because `s->a` has only
one extra unit left and `b->t` has room, so another unit can go:

```text
s->a->b->t sends 1
```

Total becomes `5`, which is also the total capacity leaving `s` (`3+2`), so it
is maximum. This small example shows why residual paths may combine edges that
were not part of the first obvious augmenting paths.

## Residual edge meaning

If an original edge has capacity `7` and currently carries flow `5`, the
residual graph contains:

```text
forward capacity 2
backward capacity 5
```

The backward capacity does not mean the original graph had a reverse road. It
means the algorithm may cancel up to `5` units of previous flow if that enables
a better global routing.

## Flow debugging tests

Use tiny graphs:

```text
single edge s->t
two parallel paths
bottleneck in the middle
disconnected sink
edge that requires rerouting through a residual edge
```

For matching, test one left vertex connected to many right vertices and many
left vertices competing for one right vertex. These cases reveal whether the
augmenting DFS actually reassigns matches.

# Exercises

## Residual graphs before code

A flow assigns a value to each directed edge, never exceeding capacity and
conserving flow at every non-source, non-sink vertex. The residual graph stores
what can still change: a forward edge has residual capacity `capacity-flow`; a
reverse edge has residual capacity `flow` and can undo an earlier choice.

Consider edges `s->a` capacity 2, `a->t` capacity 2, and `s->t` capacity 1.
Send two units through `s-a-t`, then one through `s-t`: flow is 3. A forward
edge with residual zero is saturated; its reverse edge has residual equal to
the sent amount. Omitting reverse edges makes later rerouting impossible.

### Dinic's two invariants

BFS assigns `level[v]`, the shortest residual distance from source. DFS may use
only edges with positive residual capacity and `level[to]=level[v]+1`. A DFS
phase ends when it has made the level graph blocking: every source-to-sink path
in it contains a saturated edge. Then BFS again. When sink is unreachable, no
augmenting path remains, so max-flow/min-cut proves optimality.

```text
while BFS reaches sink:
    reset every current-edge pointer
    repeatedly DFS along level-increasing residual edges
    add each pushed amount to answer
```

Current-edge pointers remember edges that have already failed in the current
level graph. Without them, repeated DFS calls revisit dead work.

### Matching is augmenting paths without capacities

For a bipartite graph, `match_right[v]` is the left owner of right vertex `v`,
or none. A DFS from a left vertex tries an unused right vertex. If it is owned,
recursively move that owner first; a successful chain is an augmenting path and
increases matching size by one.

Trace with edges `L1-R1,R2`, `L2-R1`: match L1 to R1. For L2, R1 is occupied,
so retry L1 through R2, then assign L2-R1. The matching grows from one to two.
Reset `visited[right]` for each new left root; otherwise one failed search can
incorrectly block a later one.

### Min-cut reachable side

After maximum flow, BFS from source through positive-residual edges. Call the
reachable vertices S. No residual forward edge leaves S, otherwise its endpoint
would be reachable. Thus every original edge from S to its complement is
saturated; this cut has capacity equal to the flow and is minimum.

### Language notes, checks, and workflow

Capacities and total flow use `long long` in C++. Python recursion in a deep
Dinic DFS may need a higher recursion limit in larger variants. Keep reverse
edge indices rather than searching for a reverse edge.

1. Why does a reverse residual edge have capacity equal to current flow? It
   represents exactly how much of that earlier decision can be cancelled.
2. In matching, what must be reset per DFS root? The visited-right array.
3. Why must min-cut reachability use the final residual graph? The original
   graph contains saturated edges that can no longer cross the cut.

```bash
CP_TARGET=solution python3 sections/45_flows_and_matchings/check.py
```

Test no source-sink path, parallel edges, a bottleneck, rerouting-required
matching, and a graph where source alone is the residual reachable side.

- A. Max Flow: Given a directed capacitated graph from node 1 to node n, print the maximum flow.
- B. Bipartite Matching: Given edges between left and right parts, print the maximum matching size.
- C. Min Cut Reachable Side: After max flow from 1 to n, print the flow value and the source-side reachable vertices in the residual graph.
